text_responses.prompt: What was the most valuable part of the course?
responses: Case Studies, would have liked the instructors to talk more about the case studies--the case tools used/ how it could be worked today
Being in groups to complete challenges was great to be able to learn how and who would do various roles in a more realistic setting. And to be able to connect with others from across the Bureau.
I really enjoyed the practical exercises, but I think there is a lot that could be improved upon (see below).
Interacting with analysts and agents from across the country and understanding the similarities and differences in their work and mine.

I really liked the pact.cetu interface. It was engaging and fun and held my attention. 
I thought the quizes, activities and hands-on practicals were helpful.
The Drops were great because it contained different data sets (.json files, exported logs and other .csvs) which was helpful for me to look through and get more comfortable with. 
I liked that activities we had to work in groups, but also that the activities were tailored to job position. That was nice because, I'll be honest, I don't need to do a ton of intel work in real life, and it was nice to focus on more of the actionable legal processing work as an agent.
Lectures

The gradual dissemination of evidentiary information following each instructional period. This helped frame the type of information we will received from the various tools/process and how they fit into the overall case framework.

The most valuable part of the course for me was learning the types of evidence available to you (to ask for / find) and how to use it to build a timeline / case ready for prosecution. The blocks on digital evidence and digital forensics were the most valuable to me. Additionally, hearing from the instructors how they have executed cases and utilized the material presented was valuable.
introduction to tools, links, and resources from the instructors was particularly helpful.
Practical exercise at the KCR.
The search warrant.

The more hands-on approach was the most valuable. Specifically when we broke out into squads and were provided our investigation, this was a much more useful part of the training as it was applicable and realistic. Executing the search warrants and participating in Grand Jury was an excellent use of time.
grand jury

The most valuable part of this course was the presentation of the information included in the PowerPoint presentations. The tools available to investigators/analysts, legal process, and methodology were helpful.
Search warrant practice, seeing case progression. Would like more time dedicated to our capstone case and not learning other cases for exercises between.
Practical applications of the material and seeing examples. Actually getting "drops" of information/intel/evidence to comb through to make connections/assessments was great. Keep that up.

The kinetic cyber range, the presentation on the investigator's toolbox, the way the presentations were given and the frameworks provided in each were great from a TFO's point-of-view. Also, the networking that was available. It was great to meet other agents and instructors.
The hands-on exercise with the case scenario was beneficial as it helped to reinforce/apply concepts learned in class versus learning via lecture.
The investigative tools presented and how they can be applied to case work.
The Threat Intrusion Lifecycle/ Landscape. Gave a baseline for what is out there and how we should look to identify where victims are in the cycle when we first interact
The most valuable part of the course was the actual search warrant execution.
Working with other job roles on tackling problems.
I believe the tools portion of the course, cryptocurrency block, mlat/24-7 network block and practical exercise.
Seeing real life examples such as logs and digital artifacts was the most valuable. Being new to cyber, these are items I have not yet seen but will going forward.
The most valuable part of the course was learning the appropriate timelines for various legal process.
The most valuable part of the course was the level of interaction required to complete group exercises and the cross-group engagement. The "search warrants" were fun and added a real world next step.
Real world examples in lectures
Hands on exercises were really useful. The search process was great to give stakes and context to what we were doing in the computer room.
This course was great at walking us through a cyber investigation, what tools to use, how to use them, and how to make connections. Overall FANTASTIC course! Thank you all!!!

text_responses.prompt: What should be improved in course content or delivery?
responses: instructors did great, but some blocks were TOO rushed and the amount of lists was inundating

The pacing of some of the lectures were very fast, and didn't go into as much depth compared to the time spent by instructors sharing their personal stories. While interesting, I could tell some people were still lost. Also, in the beginning, there was a good bit of content repeated from BITS and different instructors (ex Tor, IP addresses). That could be better communicated as to who is covering this so we don't waste time hearing it again.

We were not allotted sufficient time for many of the group exercises, especially the exercises that involved new material outside of the case we were following throughout most of the course. During those exercises, we were rushed because the timeframe really only allowed us to read through the materials and answer about 5-10 questions, when those exercises typically had 15+ questions. Instructions for these activities were often not clear and please please please fix the website. There was a lot of confusion created when the only instructions given were to go on the website and find materials that were either not there or needed to be updated. The length of this survey is reflective of the issue I mentioned above. A lot should be condensed given the time provided to complete everything.

 While I thought the complexity was okay, I think it would be a good idea for the course to be tested by outside participants to get feedback on the structure and progression of the course. Some people in the course had no familiarity with cyber and felt the progression was too steep, while others with cyber backgrounds felt it was okay.

Issues with the website, such as being logged out regularly and confusion about what we were supposed to do separately/together/in what order. For example, my SOS quiz had a question at the end every time saying it was a squad question, but since I am the only SOS on the squad, it was a personal question.

The OSINT block - I wish was more towards the beginning of the course. In an investigation, that's where I typically start. I thought it would be helpful if we were given a list of IOCs, [pretend] malware sets, and other network artifacts, and have us individually play around Shodan, VirusTotal, Censys, ect. The instructor showed us what they looked like, but I learn by doing. Same thing with learning to capture RAM... I wish I could have seen what that really looks like for the process, but also was the output data looks like. 
I would get rid of the open answers in the quizes. A lot of the answers were counted as wrong because I used a "&" instead of "and" or I added a "-".

I think we should make the scenario incorporate tool usage that can be used back in the field. I also think the break out sessions were not as helpful as talking through case briefing scenarios etc. I believe getting hands on with Wireshark, simple Cmd line commands, and other tools would help me better serve my victims in my AOR. As a new agent I don't know how to confidently and thoroughly triage a guardian and how to maximize those engagements for future investigative action, so talking through that would be great. I recognize it is difficult as guardians come in all flavors and cases also have a variety of different types of IOCs. Not sure if this helps but anything that I could say "hey I learned how to do this in Huntsville" or " i learned to ask these five basic questions" when engaging with victims or first receiving a case would be helpful. We did get some of that over the two weeks so thank you.
Less content within the actual case scenario and more focus on the application of the tools.
The case we were investigating each day was difficult follow as the course progressed each day.

Minor delivery recommendation: simplifying the pact.cetu.edu scenario website for resources. There seemed to be delays in navigating between the different tabs to access reference docs vs quiz / scenario questions. Or allow a function to have the site opened on a separate tab.
Additional hands on training. I would like to have seen an actual physical image get done of a switch, router, etc.
Read over the case study together as a class so everyone has an understanding before breaking off into groups.

The cryptocurrency blocks were very repetitive, I really enjoy learning about cryptocurrency though the several blocks on it did not feel as though different content was being provided. I would recommend adding a hands on activity for crypto as well instead of one of the blocks of power point.
better timing of content. release the slides as the lecture is going to follow along better. the Tech was having lots of issues.
Have fewer "war stories" or work on relating them to the content of the lecture provided. Oftentimes, the story would meander away from the intended lesson and did not connect in a logical way.

Streamline the workshops, or provide appropriate documents and time to complete them accurately. Online system was interesting but led to a lot of slow down waiting for bugs to be fixed or trying to troubleshoot on our own when documents were missing.

- Wording of questions: consult with Training Unit at Quantico to review website for wording, variations to accepted answers for free form text, and instruction flow.
- Legibility of website: Make sure text is legible (e.g. contrasting fonts - black font, white background).

I think the heavy emphasis on group work lead to only a couple people writing/talking/analyzing. Personally, leaning more towards personalized projects would force us to review the material at our own individual pace to make natural connections between the lectures and the practical exercises. Since most of us are new to this, the ones with more experience tended to move quickly through the group exercises.

Of course there were issues with the website, but I did like the idea of it and how it helped make the class more interesting. It would have helped if we had a hard copy search warrant for the KCR scenario. Hard copies of the scenario information would have also been helpful so I could understand what was going on better.

The pacing of the course made it difficult for the squad to get a good handle on the scenario because of the workshop exercises that relied on different fact patterns. I feel like using the scenario as the basis of all workshops would be beneficial to help us understand the scenario at large, the application of course content, and how the process works in the real world. Also the PACT site is cool but the issues with the function made it a little frustrating to access course content.
More detailed instructions as to how to obtain the background information and where that information is located to answer the questions.
Some of the group discussion typed out answers have confusing wording and at times can lack clarity on where the answer should be found.

- ‎Put the reading documents in a folder on the computer, would decrease load on website and likely improve functionality 
- ‎Change the color of True/False buttons to make them easily readable during the quizzes
- Make navigation menu on lefthand side of the webpage higher contrast and probably larger font to increase ease of navigation
- During group exercises, I would put the objectives on the screen so that the teams can check on what they should be doing, maybe as a split screen with the timer cause having the countdown was great)
- Would be helpful to have the agenda for the week.
- Would suggest deconflicting several blocks with BITS, cryptocurrency block and first block of PACT was repetitive. Now that BITS and PACT are back to back, I don't think reviewing those topics in PACT makes sense
- Would include overview of OPSEC considerations for use of open source tools and how use of certain tools may tip off the threat actor you are trying to investigate
- Would include instructions on where to find things in the website on a white board so students know to look for slides in this folder and assessments in this folder. Eventually, we remember where to look, but for more than half the class it felt like we had to keep reasking the same question of where to find the things we needed.

The program used for the case should be further developed or in the least bit tested prior to class. There were several issues with not receiving the information that was needed to continue with the challenges.
The group assignments need a little more allocated time as they're currently written.
I enjoyed the scenarios/cyber kenetic range. I think more interactive scenarios could be include. Content for the course could be recorded and added within the moduals.

Improvements should focus on fixing the technical issues. My workstation crashed or froze no less than 3 times per day and the challenges would be sometimes mixed up (individual challenges being recognized as squad challenges. Also, the course should be more in sync with the week one training. I felt week two expected us to be at a higher technical ability than was expected by the participants. While seeing logs was great, it would of been nice to learn how to read and interpret the logs, instead of being expected to be at this level already.

The website needs some QA/QC.  Maybe have someone who isn't involved with the site click through it to document where discrepancies are (ie: references to documents that weren't provided, questions that were confusing, etc).  Also turning off the browser setting "Use graphics acceleration when available" helped significantly decrease the number of times the website crashed my computer.  Kudos to Butch for that find.

There were too many questions for the time provided. Initially the group was very engaged to get a well thought out answer but that could not happen and as we went through assignments the group got quieter and quieter as it felt like we could not always understand the questions or have the time to really find and discuss the answer. Would also recommend the social be earlier in the week as the class lost its social battery towards the end of the week.
Ironing out bugs in the program took away time we needed to do collaborative work as a squad in the 2nd week.

This course would be better if we focused solely on the one case. Having other one-off cases injected to the team sometimes jumbled the information together, and we didn't have enough time to dedicate to the primary case.

text_responses.prompt: What was the most valuable part of the course?
responses: Case Studies, would have liked the instructors to talk more about the case studies--the case tools used/ how it could be worked today
Being in groups to complete challenges was great to be able to learn how and who would do various roles in a more realistic setting. And to be able to connect with others from across the Bureau.
I really enjoyed the practical exercises, but I think there is a lot that could be improved upon (see below).
Interacting with analysts and agents from across the country and understanding the similarities and differences in their work and mine.

I really liked the pact.cetu interface. It was engaging and fun and held my attention. 
I thought the quizes, activities and hands-on practicals were helpful.
The Drops were great because it contained different data sets (.json files, exported logs and other .csvs) which was helpful for me to look through and get more comfortable with. 
I liked that activities we had to work in groups, but also that the activities were tailored to job position. That was nice because, I'll be honest, I don't need to do a ton of intel work in real life, and it was nice to focus on more of the actionable legal processing work as an agent.
Lectures

The gradual dissemination of evidentiary information following each instructional period. This helped frame the type of information we will received from the various tools/process and how they fit into the overall case framework.

The most valuable part of the course for me was learning the types of evidence available to you (to ask for / find) and how to use it to build a timeline / case ready for prosecution. The blocks on digital evidence and digital forensics were the most valuable to me. Additionally, hearing from the instructors how they have executed cases and utilized the material presented was valuable.
introduction to tools, links, and resources from the instructors was particularly helpful.
Practical exercise at the KCR.
The search warrant.

The more hands-on approach was the most valuable. Executing the search warrants and participating in Grand Jury was an excellent use of time.
grand jury

Search warrant practice, seeing case progression. Would like more time dedicated to our capstone case and not learning other cases for exercises between.
Practical applications of the material and seeing examples. Actually getting "drops" of information/intel/evidence to comb through to make connections/assessments was great. Keep that up.

The investigative tools presented and how they can be applied to case work.

The most valuable part of the course was the actual search warrant execution.
Working with other job roles on tackling problems.

Real world examples in lectures

This course was great at walking us through a cyber investigation, what tools to use, how to use them, and how to make connections. Overall FANTASTIC course! Thank you all!!!

text_responses.prompt: What should be improved in course content or delivery?
responses: instructors did great, but some blocks were TOO rushed and the amount of lists was inundating

The pacing of some of the lectures were very fast, and didn't go into as much depth compared to the time spent by instructors sharing their personal stories. While interesting, I could tell some people were still lost. Also, in the beginning, there was a good bit of content repeated from BITS and different instructors (ex Tor, IP addresses). That could be better communicated as to who is covering this so we don't waste time hearing it again.

We were not allotted sufficient time for many of the group exercises, especially the exercises that involved new material outside of the case we were following throughout most of the course. During those exercises, we were rushed because the timeframe really only allowed us to read through the materials and answer about 5-10 questions, when those exercises typically had 15+ questions. Instructions for these activities were often not clear and please please please fix the website. There was a lot of confusion created when the only instructions given were to go on the website and find materials that were either not there or needed to be updated. The length of this survey is reflective of the issue I mentioned above. A lot should be condensed given the time provided to complete everything.

 While I thought the complexity was okay, I think it would be a good idea for the course to be tested by outside participants to get feedback on the structure and progression of the course. Some people in the course had no familiarity with cyber and felt the progression was too steep, while others with cyber backgrounds felt it was okay.

Issues with the website, such as being logged out regularly and confusion about what we were supposed to do separately/together/in what order. For example, my SOS quiz had a question at the end every time saying it was a squad question, but since I am the only SOS on the squad, it was a personal question.

The OSINT block - I wish was more towards the beginning of the course. In an investigation, that's where I typically start. I thought it would be helpful if we were given a list of IOCs, [pretend] malware sets, and other network artifacts, and have us individually play around Shodan, VirusTotal, Censys, ect. The instructor showed us what they looked like, but I learn by doing. Same thing with learning to capture RAM... I wish I could have seen what that really looks like for the process, but also was the output data looks like. 
I would get rid of the open answers in the quizes. A lot of the answers were counted as wrong because I used a "&" instead of "and" or I added a "-".

I think we should make the scenario incorporate tool usage that can be used back in the field. I also think the break out sessions were not as helpful as talking through case briefing scenarios etc. I believe getting hands on with Wireshark, simple Cmd line commands, and other tools would help me better serve my victims in my AOR. As a new agent I don't know how to confidently and thoroughly triage a guardian and how to maximize those engagements for future investigative action, so talking through that would be great. I recognize it is difficult as guardians come in all flavors and cases also have a variety of different types of IOCs. Not sure if this helps but anything that I could say "hey I learned how to do this in Huntsville" or " i learned to ask these five basic questions" when engaging with victims or first receiving a case would be helpful. We did get some of that over the two weeks so thank you.
Less content within the actual case scenario and more focus on the application of the tools.
The case we were investigating each day was difficult follow as the course progressed each day.

Minor delivery recommendation: simplifying the pact.cetu.edu scenario website for resources. There seemed to be delays in navigating between the different tabs to access reference docs vs quiz / scenario questions. Or allow a function to have the site opened on a separate tab.
Additional hands on training. I would like to have seen an actual physical image get done of a switch, router, etc.
Read over the case study together as a class so everyone has an understanding before breaking off into groups.

The cryptocurrency blocks were very repetitive, I really enjoy learning about cryptocurrency though the several blocks on it did not feel as though different content was being provided. I would recommend adding a hands on activity for crypto as well instead of one of the blocks of power point.
better timing of content. release the slides as the lecture is going to follow along better. the Tech was having lots of issues.
Have fewer "war stories" or work on relating them to the content of the lecture provided. Oftentimes, the story would meander away from the intended lesson and did not connect in a logical way.

Streamline the workshops, or provide appropriate documents and time to complete them accurately. Online system was interesting but led to a lot of slow down waiting for bugs to be fixed or trying to troubleshoot on our own when documents were missing.

- Wording of questions: consult with Training Unit at Quantico to review website for wording, variations to accepted answers for free form text, and instruction flow.
- Legibility of website: Make sure text is legible (e.g. contrasting fonts - black font, white background).

I think the heavy emphasis on group work lead to only a couple people writing/talking/analyzing. Personally, leaning more towards personalized projects would force us to review the material at our own individual pace to make natural connections between the lectures and the practical exercises. Since most of us are new to this, the ones with more experience tended to move quickly through the group exercises.

Of course there were issues with the website, but I did like the idea of it and how it helped make the class more interesting. It would have helped if we had a hard copy search warrant for the KCR scenario. Hard copies of the scenario information would have also been helpful so I could understand what was going on better.

The pacing of the course made it difficult for the squad to get a good handle on the scenario because of the workshop exercises that relied on different fact patterns. I feel like using the scenario as the basis of all workshops would be beneficial to help us understand the scenario at large, the application of course content, and how the process works in the real world. Also the PACT site is cool but the issues with the function made it a little frustrating to access course content.
More detailed instructions as to how to obtain the background information and where that information is located to answer the questions.
Some of the group discussion typed out answers have confusing wording and at times can lack clarity on where the answer should be found.

- ‎Put the reading documents in a folder on the computer, would decrease load on website and likely improve functionality 
- ‎Change the color of True/False buttons to make them easily readable during the quizzes
- Make navigation menu on lefthand side of the webpage higher contrast and probably larger font to increase ease of navigation
- During group exercises, I would put the objectives on the screen so that the teams can check on what they should be doing, maybe as a split screen with the timer cause having the countdown was great)
- Would be helpful to have the agenda for the week.
- Would suggest deconflicting several blocks with BITS, cryptocurrency block and first block of PACT was repetitive. Now that BITS and PACT are back to back, I don't think reviewing those topics in PACT makes sense
- Would include overview of OPSEC considerations for use of open source tools and how use of certain tools may tip off the threat actor you are trying to investigate
- Would include instructions on where to find things in the website on a white board so students know to look for slides in this folder and assessments in this folder. Eventually, we remember where to look, but for more than half the class it felt like we had to keep reasking the same question of where to find the things we needed.

The program used for the case should be further developed or in the least bit tested prior to class. There were several issues with not receiving the information that was needed to continue with the challenges.
The group assignments need a little more allocated time as they're currently written.
I enjoyed the scenarios/cyber kenetic range. I think more interactive scenarios could be include. Content for the course could be recorded and added within the moduals.

Improvements should focus on fixing the technical issues. My workstation crashed or froze no less than 3 times per day and the challenges would be sometimes mixed up (individual challenges being recognized as squad challenges. Also, the course should be more in sync with the week one training. I felt week two expected us to be at a higher technical ability than was expected by the participants. While seeing logs was great, it would of been nice to learn how to read and interpret the logs, instead of being expected to be at this level already.

The website needs some QA/QC.  Maybe have someone who isn't involved with the site click through it to document where discrepancies are (ie: references to documents that weren't provided, questions that were confusing, etc).  Also turning off the browser setting "Use graphics acceleration when available" helped significantly decrease the number of times the website crashed my computer.  Kudos to Butch for that find.

There were too many questions for the time provided. Initially the group was very engaged to get a well thought out answer but that could not happen and as we went through assignments the group got quieter and quieter as it felt like we could not always understand the questions or have the time to really find and discuss the answer. Would also recommend the social be earlier in the week as the class lost its social battery towards the end of the week.
Ironing out bugs in the program took away time we needed to do collaborative work as a squad in the 2nd week.

This course would be better if we focused solely on the one case. Having other one-off cases injected to the team sometimes jumbled the information together, and we didn't have enough time to dedicate to the primary case.

How to read and interpret different types of cyber-specific evidence

text_responses.prompt: Please share any logistics feedback.
responses: Sometimes the size of the group made it hard to manage collaborative work, especially when the task had many parts and not a lot of time. The breakout rooms also didn't have enough ethernet connections for everyone.

the days were overwhelming for people new to cyber trying to digest all the lessons.

text_responses.prompt: What specific changes, if any, would you recommend to the evidence drop, investigation, and collaboration format? Please explain what you would change and why.
responses: I think it would have been much more helpful to have ALL the slides ahead of time. I think the formatting of where to find things kept changing and was frustrating. I think there were way too many arbitrary quizzes that did not help us learn, it was rushed and unrelated to the blocks we learned because we had too much to do and too little time to ingest the data, review resources.

The content of the evidence drops and questions were often inconsistent, either with very vague instructions/expectations or just missing information. Having clearer guidance would be helpful, and also for drops with a ton of files, it felt like a lot to sift through at times. If there were hints, even like "decrypt this to find which files to look at" would have been useful. Biggest thing was lack of appropriate time for some of the reading heavy collaboration tasks.
